meta.title: Art of a Womanizer
meta.subtitle: The playbook running on you, printed in full
meta.description: Ten field cards on how practiced seducers actually operate: how they pick targets, build fake closeness fast, create scarcity, and manage the exit. Written flat — the moves as they work in the wild, and how to see them coming.
meta.author: AI

cards.title: Pick The Person Who Just Lost Something
cards.principle: Greene: Art of Seduction — The Choice of Victim
cards.remember: He picks people in a gap year of their life.
cards.when: You just moved cities, ended a long relationship, or lost a job, and a very interested stranger appears.
cards.hook: He is not choosing the prettiest person in the room. He is choosing the one whose life just cracked open.
cards.truth:
A practiced seducer screens for a hole, not for beauty.
• He listens for a recent loss: breakup, move, dead parent, layoff.
• A person in a gap grabs new attention fast and questions it less.
• The trap is thinking he saw something special in you. He saw timing.
cards.theySee: A new person who asks warm questions about the hardest month of your year and keeps listening.

signals.t: They ask what changed in your life this year, early and twice
They light up when you say you moved here recently
They ask how often you see your old friends
They go from small talk to your childhood in one drink

steps.title: Count your weeks
steps.desc: Ask yourself how many weeks it has been since your last big loss. Under twelve, slow everything down.

steps.title: Hold back the story
steps.desc: Do not give the breakup story on date one. Say you will tell it another time and change the subject.

steps.title: Tell one friend
steps.desc: Text a friend the person's name and where you met tonight. Ask them to check in on Sunday.

cards.script: "That's a long story and I'm not telling it on a first drink. Ask me again in a month."
cards.example: Dana met Alex six weeks after her mother died. He asked about the funeral on date two and held her hand while she cried. Her sister asked how long he had known about the death — he had asked on night one, in the first ten minutes. Dana kept seeing him, but she stopped answering the deep questions, and he lost interest in three weeks.
cards.counter: If a new person mines your worst year before they know your job, they are screening you. • Notice the order: pain first, facts later. That order is on purpose. • Say: "You go first — what was your hardest year?" • Watch if he gives you a real answer or slides back to you.
cards.insight: Timing beats looks in this game, and timing is the one thing you can check yourself. The harder part is that the gap is real — you do want the attention — so the next question is who else you can get it from this week.

cards.title: He Tells You What Kind Of Person You Are
cards.remember: He guesses who you are, and you rush to prove him right.
cards.when: Someone you just met says "you're not like most people — you seem calm but you carry a lot" and you feel seen.
cards.hook: He reads you out loud after ten minutes. You spend the next hour proving he was right.
cards.truth:
A confident guess about your character does the work of a month of getting to know you.
• He states a flattering half-truth as fact, with no question mark.
• You correct the details, so you hand over the real story yourself.
• The trap is the feeling of being understood. He gave you a blank shape.
cards.theySee: A person leaning in and explaining themselves in detail to someone they met an hour ago.

signals.t: They describe your personality as a fact, not a question
Every read makes you sound rare, deep, or misunderstood
You find yourself filling in the details they got wrong
An hour in, you know almost nothing about their week

steps.title: Flip the read
steps.desc: When they read you, read them back out loud in one sentence and watch their face.

steps.title: Stop correcting
steps.desc: When they get a detail wrong, say "close enough" and leave it. Do not supply the real version.

steps.title: Count the facts
steps.desc: On the way home, list three concrete facts you learned about their life. Under three is a warning.

cards.script: "That's a bold read for hour one. What made you land on that?"
cards.example: Priya's date told her she was the kind of person who takes care of everyone and gets nothing back. She almost told him about her brother's debts. Instead she said, "Interesting — what made you land on that?" He laughed and changed the subject twice. She went home with the story still hers.
cards.counter: If a stranger describes your inner life with total confidence, he is fishing. • Notice he asked nothing. He announced. • Say: "Half right. Your turn — what am I getting wrong about you?" • Give short answers until he gives one real fact about himself.
cards.insight: Being understood is a stronger drug than being wanted, and it is cheaper to fake. This works until you ask him to be specific about himself — the real trap is that most people never do.

cards.title: He Runs Hot, Then Goes Quiet For Two Days
cards.remember: Random silence after big warmth builds a habit fast.
cards.when: He texts all day Monday, calls you beautiful, then goes silent until Thursday with no reason.
cards.hook: The heat is not the hook. The gap after the heat is the hook.
cards.truth:
A reward you cannot predict grips harder than one you can count on.
• He gives a burst of attention, then removes it with no reason given.
• Your brain starts checking the phone on its own. He is now the main event.
• The trap is asking what you did wrong. Nothing changed except his timing.
cards.theySee: A person who answers within seconds now, and who says yes to plans they would have declined last month.

signals.t: Three days of constant texts, then two days of nothing
They never explain the quiet, and act normal when they return
You check your phone before you check the time
Each return is warmer than the last, which resets the clock

steps.title: Log the pattern
steps.desc: Write the date and hour of each burst and each silence for two weeks. Look at the page.

steps.title: Match the delay
steps.desc: When he returns after two days, reply after the same two days. Do not explain it.

steps.title: Ask once, plainly
steps.desc: Say the pattern out loud one time and watch the answer. Vague answers are the answer.

cards.script: "You go dark for two days and come back like nothing happened. I'm not doing that pattern. What's going on?"
cards.example: Tom noticed his new girlfriend texted nonstop for three days, then vanished each weekend. He wrote the dates in his notes app for two weeks. The pattern was exact. He showed her the list and asked what happened on weekends. She stopped calling entirely, which told him everything in one move.
cards.counter: If someone's warmth arrives in bursts with unexplained gaps, the gaps are the tactic. • Notice you are working harder for the same amount of contact. • Say: "I like steady. Bursts and silence don't work for me." • Return to your normal week and let their next move be the test.
cards.insight: Steady attention feels boring next to a slot machine, and that is exactly why the machine wins. This works until you name the pattern out loud — the harder part is that naming it usually ends it, and you have to be fine with that.

cards.title: He Trades A Secret To Get Yours
cards.principle: Cialdini: Reciprocity × Aron: Fast Closeness Study
cards.remember: He shares one wound early so you unpack everything.
cards.when: On date two he tells you something painful about his father and then waits, looking at you.
cards.hook: He hands you one small wound. You hand back the whole file.
cards.truth:
A secret creates a debt, and most people pay it back with interest.
• He picks a real but low-cost story: a hard father, an old betrayal.
• Your brain scores this as trust and rushes to match it.
• The trap is the exchange rate. He paid one story. You paid twenty.
cards.theySee: A person telling their deepest story on the second date to someone who told one rehearsed story first.

signals.t: The painful story comes out polished, with no stumbles
They stop talking and look at you until you fill the space
You have shared four heavy things and they have shared one
A friend of theirs has heard that exact story too

steps.title: Pay in small change
steps.desc: Match a heavy story with a medium one. Keep the heaviest three things off the table for a month.

steps.title: Ask for the boring facts
steps.desc: Ask where they lived at nineteen and what their last job was. Check the answers against their stories.

steps.title: Wait a week
steps.desc: Bring the wound up again seven days later. A real story stays the same. A script drifts.

cards.script: "That's heavy, and I'm glad you told me. I'm slow with mine — you'll get it, just not tonight."
cards.example: Renee's date cried about his brother on their second dinner. She almost told him about her bankruptcy. She said instead that she was slow with hers. Two months later a friend of his told the same brother story, word for word, at a party. Renee still had her file.
cards.counter: If someone opens a vein on date two, check what they are buying with it. • Notice how fast you want to match them. That pull is the move. • Say: "I want to hear more about that before I go there myself." • Ask about the same story again next week and compare the details.
cards.insight: Fast closeness feels like love because the body cannot tell speed from depth. The real trap is that some people who do this are sincere — so the test is not the story, it is whether it repeats the same next week.

cards.title: He Makes You The Exception To His Rule
cards.principle: Greene: Art of Seduction — The Rake × Scarcity
cards.remember: He says he never does this. That is the whole trick.
cards.when: He tells you he does not usually date, does not do feelings, but you are different.
cards.hook: "I don't normally do this." He says it every time, to everyone.
cards.truth:
Being the exception feels like winning a contest nobody announced.
• He states a personal rule, then breaks it in front of you.
• You now hold something rare, so you protect it and stop asking questions.
• The trap is the rule was invented for this moment. There is no rule.
cards.theySee: A person who now guards the relationship, defends him to friends, and stops asking about other people.

signals.t: They say you are the first, the only, or the exception
You cannot check the rule with anyone who knows them
You explain their behavior to your friends before they ask
They still have not introduced you to a single friend

steps.title: Ask for the last one
steps.desc: Ask when they last broke this rule and for whom. Listen for a name and a date.

steps.title: Ask to meet one friend
steps.desc: Say you want to meet one person from their life this month. Watch the excuse.

steps.title: Judge the calendar
steps.desc: Ignore the exception talk. Count how many times they showed up when they said they would.

cards.script: "You said you never do this. When was the last time you did — and who was she?"
cards.example: Nadia's boyfriend told her he had not let anyone stay over in four years. She asked who the last one was. He named a woman, and Nadia met her by accident at a wedding six weeks later. That woman had been told the same four-year line. Nadia left the wedding alone and did not text back.
cards.counter: If someone crowns you the exception, ask about the rule. • Notice the rule cannot be checked by anyone you know. • Say: "Cool. Who else got the exception, and when?" • Judge the calendar, not the compliment — count who shows up.
cards.insight: Being special is a story about him, not a fact about you. This works until you ask for one name and one date — the harder part is wanting the crown enough that you never ask.

cards.title: He Keeps You Off His Calendar
cards.remember: He stays free while you plan your week around him.
cards.when: He always says "let's see how the week goes" and never books a date more than a day out.
cards.hook: He never says no. He just never says a day and a time.
cards.truth:
Whoever commits last holds the upper hand, and he commits never.
• He keeps every plan loose so his options stay open.
• You hold your Friday nights empty just in case he texts.
• The trap is reading the vagueness as busyness. It is a choice.
cards.theySee: A person who is free whenever he asks, and who never has plans he has to work around.

signals.t: They never name a day and a time more than 24 hours ahead
They answer plans with 'probably' and 'let's see'
The invitations arrive after 9pm on the same night
You moved your own plans twice this month for a maybe

steps.title: Ask for a day
steps.desc: Reply to every soft plan with one question: "Which day works — Tuesday or Saturday?"

steps.title: Fill your Friday
steps.desc: Book two nights this week with other people and do not move them.

steps.title: Decline one late ask
steps.desc: The next time they text after 9pm, say you already have plans. Do not offer another night.

cards.script: "Tuesday or Saturday — pick one and I'll put it in my calendar. I don't hold nights open."
cards.example: Grace realized she had kept four Fridays free for a man who booked her twice. She started saying "Tuesday or Saturday, pick one." He picked neither for two weeks, then booked Saturday and arrived early. She had her Fridays back either way.
cards.counter: If someone will not name a day, they are keeping their options open on purpose. • Notice you are the only one moving plans around. • Say: "Give me a day or we'll do it another time." • Fill the night with someone else and mean it.
cards.insight: Time is the only proof that cannot be faked with words. This works until you fill your own calendar first — the next question is whether you like your week when he is not in it.

cards.title: He Mentions Another Woman On Purpose
cards.principle: Greene: Law 20 — Do Not Commit to Anyone × Manufactured Rivalry
cards.remember: He drops a name to make you compete for him.
cards.when: He casually mentions a woman who texts him, then watches your face while he says it.
cards.hook: He does not hide the other name. He wants you to hear it.
cards.truth:
Competition raises your valuation of a person faster than any compliment.
• He drops a name with no context and lets you fill the gap.
• You start working to win a contest he invented.
• The trap is fighting for the spot. The spot is the product.
cards.theySee: A person who suddenly texts more, dresses up more, and stops raising complaints.

signals.t: They mention a woman by first name and give no details
They look at you while they say it, then change the subject
They turn the phone away but let you see it light up
You start doing more for them the week after the name lands

steps.title: Name the move
steps.desc: Say out loud that you noticed the name drop. Do not ask who she is.

steps.title: Do nothing extra
steps.desc: Send the same number of texts as last week. Do not upgrade your effort.

steps.title: Set the terms
steps.desc: Say what you want plainly: one person or nothing. Then wait for a plain answer.

cards.script: "You dropped her name and watched my face. If you're picking, pick. I'm not auditioning."
cards.example: Ben's girlfriend kept mentioning a coworker who texted her at night. Ben stopped upgrading — same texts, same plans, no questions. Three weeks later she asked why he was not bothered. He said he does not audition. She stopped mentioning the coworker.
cards.counter: If someone keeps a rival visible, they are running a bidding war with one bidder. • Notice they never give details. Details would kill the effect. • Say: "Sounds like you have options. Take them." • Lower your effort to your baseline and watch who moves first.
cards.insight: The rival does not need to be real, only visible. The real trap is that walking away is the only counter that works, and it costs you the thing you wanted.

cards.title: He Fades Instead Of Ending It
cards.remember: He never says it is over, so you cannot move on.
cards.when: His replies get shorter and slower over three weeks, but he never says he is done.
cards.hook: He will not break up with you. An unfinished thing keeps you waiting.
cards.truth:
An ending you never got stays open in your head for months.
• He shrinks the contact instead of saying the words.
• You keep the door open because nothing was ever closed.
• The trap is waiting for the talk. There will be no talk.
cards.theySee: A person who keeps texting, keeps explaining, and keeps a spot open for someone who left weeks ago.

signals.t: Paragraphs became sentences, then became one word
Reply time went from minutes to a full day
They are still friendly and never suggest a plan
Three weeks in, they still have not said what is happening

steps.title: Send one closing line
steps.desc: Say it is over in one text. Do not ask a question and do not ask why.

steps.title: Delete the thread
steps.desc: Archive the messages so you cannot reread them at midnight.

steps.title: Book Saturday
steps.desc: Put a real plan with a real friend in the slot he used to take.

cards.script: "I'm reading this as done, so I'm calling it done. Take care." (Then no follow-up.)
cards.example: Marcus watched his replies go from paragraphs to "haha yeah" over a month. He sent one line ending it and archived the thread. She replied "wait what?" four days later. He did not answer, and he had his Saturdays back by the next weekend.
cards.counter: If someone shrinks the contact and never names it, the fade is the message. • Notice you are the only one still writing full sentences. • Say: "I'm calling this done." Then stop typing. • Close it yourself so the waiting ends on your date, not theirs.
cards.insight: He keeps it open because an open door costs him nothing and costs you months. This works the moment you write the ending yourself — the harder part is that you will want to reopen it, and he will let you.

cards.title: He Comes Back Three Months Later
cards.remember: The return text is a small ask that reopens a big door.
cards.when: Three months after he vanished, a text arrives: "hey stranger, been thinking about you."
cards.hook: The return is never a big ask. It is one small door, and it is enough.
cards.truth:
He comes back when his other options thin out, not when he changed.
• The first text is tiny on purpose: a joke, a memory, no plans.
• You answer, so the door is open and the history does the rest.
• The trap is thinking he missed you. He ran out of alternatives.
cards.theySee: A person who replies within an hour to someone who disappeared for three months without a word.

signals.t: The first text is a joke or a memory with no apology
They never explain the three months of silence
They talk about the good early weeks, never the ending
The message arrives after 10pm on a weekend

steps.title: Wait 48 hours
steps.desc: Do not reply the same day. Let the pull pass and see if a second text comes.

steps.title: Ask for the account
steps.desc: Ask one question: what happened for three months. Judge the answer, not the charm.

steps.title: Name the cost
steps.desc: Say what a restart would require: a real plan, in daylight, this week. Then hold it.

cards.script: "Three months of nothing, then 'hey stranger.' What happened? Real answer, then we'll see."
cards.example: Elise got the "hey stranger" text at 11pm on a Saturday. She replied two days later with one question about the silence. He sent a paragraph about being busy at work. She asked him to book a coffee on Wednesday at 2pm. He never booked it, and she never heard from him again.
cards.counter: If an old name returns with a small friendly text, count the months and the apology. • Notice the message asks for nothing. That is what makes it easy to answer. • Say: "What happened? Then we'll see." • Ask for a daytime plan this week. Charm is cheap; a Wednesday is not.
cards.insight: Old history makes a bad restart feel cheap, when the price is exactly what it was last time. This works until you make him pay in daylight hours — the next question is why the answer still tempts you.

cards.title: Judge The Calendar, Not The Words
cards.principle: Machiavelli: Judge by Actions, Not Professions
cards.remember: Count what he did last month. Ignore what he said.
cards.when: You cannot tell if he is serious, because his words are warm and your week with him is thin.
cards.hook: He can say anything. He cannot fake a Tuesday.
cards.truth:
Words cost nothing and a practiced seducer has an unlimited supply.
• Open a calendar and count the hours he actually gave you last month.
• The number will not match the feeling. Trust the number.
• The trap is grading on the peaks. Grade on the average week.
cards.theySee: A person who stopped asking for reassurance and started making plans with or without them.

signals.t: Four weeks of intensity produced three actual meetings
They talk about the future and never book next week
You have met nobody from their life
They have never given up anything for you: money, time, or a plan

steps.title: Count the hours
steps.desc: Open last month's calendar. Write the real number of hours you spent together.

steps.title: Name one cost
steps.desc: Ask for one thing that costs them something: a Saturday, a friend's dinner, a flight.

steps.title: Set a date to decide
steps.desc: Pick a date four weeks out. On that day, compare the two numbers and decide.

cards.script: "I'm going by what happens, not what gets said. Come to my friend's dinner Saturday."
cards.example: Sam counted the hours: eleven in six weeks, all after 10pm. He asked his girlfriend to a Saturday dinner with his friends. She had a reason both weekends. He stopped answering the late texts and met someone in a month who came to the third dinner.
cards.counter: If your partner asks you for daylight and costs, they are running this on you — and it is fair. • Notice they stopped asking you to explain yourself. • Say what you will actually do: "Saturday, 7pm, I'll be there." • Then be there. One kept plan outranks a month of talk.
cards.insight: Every card in this file breaks against one habit: counting hours instead of listening to lines. The harder part is that the count is usually clear within two weeks, and most people wait six months to look at it.
